cim: North Dakota committee advances AI protections, weighs data center regulations
cim_eredeti: North Dakota committee advances AI protections, weighs data center regulations
szoveg_eredeti:
BISMARCK, N.D. – North Dakota’s interim Artificial Intelligence and Data Center Committee voted Tuesday to advance a proposal establishing AI consumer protections and a state Artificial Intelligence Council, while leaving a separate chatbot bill for additional work before the 2027 legislative session.

The committee recommended the broader AI bill to Legislative Management after discussing concerns about privacy, enforcement and the makeup of the proposed council. Members emphasized that the draft remains subject to revisions.

The proposal would require AI systems interacting with consumers to disclose that users are communicating with artificial intelligence. It also would prohibit developing or deploying AI with the intent to encourage self-harm, harm to others or criminal activity, and restrict certain uses of biometric data to identify individuals without consent.

The attorney general would enforce the proposed consumer protections.

The bill also would establish a supervised testing program allowing developers to test innovative AI systems for a limited time without obtaining certain regulatory authorizations. Participants would submit quarterly reports to the Information Technology Department.

A proposed seven-member AI council would examine the technology’s development and recommend changes to state laws and regulations.

Representative Mary Schneider questioned language giving the attorney general exclusive enforcement authority and preventing private lawsuits under the proposal. She said parents or other people harmed by AI may need a way to bring their own cases.

Senator Janne Myrdal said those questions deserve further consideration during the legislative session.

“It’s a good start, but it’s certainly not a final bill,” Myrdal said.

A separate proposal addressing companion chatbots did not advance as a committee bill. Instead, lawmakers agreed to continue refining it for possible introduction by an individual legislator.

That draft would require chatbots to identify themselves as artificial intelligence at the beginning of each interaction and at least every three hours during continuous adult use. For minors, reminders would be required at least hourly.

It also would require protocols addressing mental and behavioral health concerns, referrals to crisis resources and measures to prevent content encouraging or explaining self-harm or harm to others.

Additional provisions would prohibit manipulative engagement tactics directed at minors and require reasonable measures to prevent chatbots from producing material depicting sexual conduct for those users.

Committee members discussed whether the language adequately covers AI-enabled toys and whether parents should receive additional information about their children’s interactions.

The committee also reviewed developing proposals to regulate data centers, including a plan outlined by Representative Anna Novak focused on electricity costs, water use and what happens to facilities when operations end.

Novak described the electricity portion as a “bring your own power” approach intended to ensure residential customers do not pay electricity or infrastructure costs attributable to data centers or other large electricity users.

She said the proposal remains under development, with differences between investor-owned utilities and rural electric cooperatives complicating the framework.

Novak also proposed requiring closed-loop water systems and establishing standards for removing equipment and preparing former data centers for other uses. She said requiring entire buildings to be demolished would be wasteful unless local ordinances required it.

Under the approach she outlined, zoning decisions would remain local, followed by state permitting if a community approves a project.

Several members questioned whether new requirements should apply specifically to data centers or more broadly to large industrial electricity users. Others raised concerns about imposing reclamation requirements on data centers that do not apply to other industries.

Senator Dean Rummel suggested narrowing data center sales tax exemptions to computer technology, removing exemptions for items such as cooling systems, racks and fiber optics.

The committee discussed those concepts without advancing a completed data center bill. Additional proposals are expected to be developed by individual lawmakers for the next session.
